strengths: The paper addresses a relevant continual-segmentation problem: preserving previous classes while improving minority-class performance and representing multiple future classes. Combining prototype retention with learned cluster assignment is potentially useful.

Evaluation spans three datasets, multiple incremental schedules, and convolutional and Transformer architectures. Matched-architecture results are encouraging: DeepLab-V3 achieves 36.4 versus 34.9 mIoU for RCIL+LGKD on ADE20K 100-10, and 62.41 versus 59.25 for SSUL on VOC 10-1 (Tables 5–6).

Table 1 provides direct empirical support for the modified loss. On ADE20K 100-50, overall mIoU improves from 34.8 to 37.9 and minority-class mIoU from 26.4 to 30.8, while majority-class performance also improves. The majority–minority gap consequently decreases.

The ablations examine several relevant choices, including loss scaling, adaptive versus fixed visual grammar, cluster margins, neighborhood size, and backbones. The supplement supplies an algorithm, optimization settings, and an explicit limitations discussion.
weaknesses: The central fairness interpretation does not follow from Propositions 1–2. These results characterize optimal normalized probability allocations, but Section 3.2 interprets smaller per-feature probability as stronger attraction and greater geometric compactness. Duplicating identical features decreases their normalized probabilities without changing cluster compactness. Consequently, shrinking differences between these probabilities does not establish the claimed fairness mechanism, although Table 1 supports empirical benefits.

There are consequential ambiguities in the objective and its optimization. Proposition 2 assumes that feature probabilities and the transition-vector probability share a normalized total, but Eq. (4) does not specify inclusion of the transition vector in its denominator. With the stated feature-only denominator and an unconstrained vector, its loss term is unbounded below. Furthermore, Eq. (8) optimizes network parameters while the cluster centers are described as frozen or momentum-updated. Under that procedure, the center-only regularizer has no gradient to the network; no differentiable update explaining its reported ablation gains is specified.

The supplementary knowledge-distillation argument is also unsupported. Eqs. (16)–(17) invoke a metric's triangle inequality and then identify its distance with the contrastive loss, without establishing that this loss is a metric. The subsequent Big-O manipulation does not establish the claimed distillation guarantee. This weakens the theoretical account of forgetting prevention, although the retention results remain useful empirical evidence.

The experiments only partly isolate the proposed contributions. Section 4.2 states that removing visual grammar also reduces the unknown-cluster count to one, confounding that ablation. Table 4 supports adaptive assignment, but the configuration of a matched multiple-cluster nearest-assignment baseline is insufficiently clear. Comparisons against simpler class-balanced losses would also help establish the contribution beyond the cited parametric contrastive learning and ClusFormer components. Unknown-class separation is illustrated qualitatively in Figure 6 without quantitative cluster-assignment evaluation.

Reproducibility remains limited by missing DBSCAN density parameters, insufficient detail on selecting unknown pixels when background also contains previous classes, and an underspecified ImageNet visual-grammar pretraining procedure. The majority/minority partitions across datasets and computational overhead are also insufficiently documented. The unresolved objective and training-specification issues are the concerns that tip the recommendation toward weak rejection despite the substantial positive benchmark evidence; presentation refinements are secondary.
